name: Cutting

card.summary: A calorie-deficit phase to lose fat and show muscle and bone definition; a staple of looksmaxxing leanness advice.
card.note: Aggressive deficits carry muscle-loss and hormonal risks, and forum questions about cutting during puberty raise additional concerns.

quick.overview:
Cutting is eating in a calorie deficit to lose body fat while trying to keep muscle. In bodybuilding it is the phase before a contest, typically lasting a few months, and it is alternated with bulking.

In looksmaxxing it is the main way users try to lower body fat for a more defined face and body. Forums include many teenagers asking how aggressive a cut can be during puberty.
quick.mechanism: Intake is set below maintenance, usually with resistance training and high protein to preserve muscle. A larger deficit speeds loss but raises the risk of losing muscle. A Grokipedia summary cites deficits of about 10 to 20 percent below maintenance and a loss rate of 0.5 to 1 percent of bodyweight per week.
quick.risks: Larger deficits raise the risk of muscle loss, and the same summary links prolonged low energy availability to impaired hormonal function, fatigue and mood changes. Whether the cut is worthwhile if muscle is lost is described as unclear. Posts by minors asking about extreme deficits during puberty are common on forums.

lead: Cutting is a phase of eating in a net negative energy balance, a calorie deficit, to lose body fat while keeping as much muscle as possible.[1][2] Its appearance payoff is definition: as fat covers less of the muscles and bones beneath, the waist, abdomen, jawline and cheeks look sharper, and the muscle built in earlier training phases becomes visible.[1][2] In competitive bodybuilding, athletes typically spend an off-season building muscle and then cut for roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest.[1]

The method spread from bodybuilding into general fitness and then into looksmaxxing, where it is discussed as the route to a leaner, more angular face and a more V-shaped torso, often under the label leanmaxxing.[3][4][5] Research on perception supports the link between fat and the face: a review with a meta-analysis found that observers can estimate body mass reasonably well from facial cues alone (summary r = 0.71 across 458 participants), and a separate experiment found that people lowered a face's apparent adiposity to make it look more attractive.[11]

The sports-nutrition literature describes cutting in terms of rate and protection of lean tissue. A 2014 review for natural bodybuilders suggests losing about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight per week, with high protein and continued resistance training, and flags eating-disorder risk among competitors.[9] A 2011 trial in elite athletes compared slower and faster weight loss and found larger fat loss and a gain in lean mass in the slower group.[11] Reviews of low energy availability describe hormonal and bone consequences when intake falls too far below what training demands.[10]

In online communities cutting threads concern appetite, carbohydrate restriction, how much a drop from the mid-teens to low body fat percentages changes a face, and, frequently, whether teenagers can cut during puberty.[3][4][5][7][8]

chain: Eat below maintenance so stored fat is used for energy
Body fat falls while resistance training signals the body to keep muscle
Face, jaw and abdomen look more defined and muscle becomes visible
angle.text: Cutting lowers body fat, which changes how the face and body read: jaw and cheekbone contours show more clearly and trained muscle becomes visible. Users combine it with resistance training and high protein so that most of the weight lost is fat rather than muscle.

infobox: About 8-16 weeks; competitive prep about 12-14 weeks [1][2]
About 0.5-1% of body weight per week [9]
Leanmaxxing, mini-cut, recomp, diet break, refeed

paras: Cutting is the fat-loss phase that follows a building phase in bodybuilding. Wikipedia describes bulking as eating in a calorie surplus and cutting as eating in a deficit, and notes that a larger deficit burns fat faster but raises the risk of losing muscle.[1] Preparation for a show combines a sub-maintenance diet with cardiovascular exercise, and in the final stage competitors use carbohydrate loading and dehydration to maximise definition and vascularity.[1]

The word also appears in general weight-loss discussion, where energy deficit is the core mechanism and the weight lost can include lean mass such as muscle.[6] In looksmaxxing usage the goal is usually a lower body-fat percentage for aesthetic reasons rather than a competition date, and a cut is often followed by a maintenance or lean-gaining phase.

Organised physique contests date to the turn of the twentieth century: Eugen Sandow staged his Great Competition at the Royal Albert Hall on 14 September 1901, and Bernarr Macfadden promoted a large contest in New York at the turn of 1903 to 1904.[1] Joe and Ben Weider founded the IFBB in 1946, Mr. Olympia began in 1965, and the 1977 film Pumping Iron brought Arnold Schwarzenegger and other competitors to a wide audience.[1] A Grokipedia summary says the cutting phase was popularised in the 1970s through that era of bodybuilding and later absorbed more formal nutrition such as carbohydrate cycling.[2]

From competitive bodybuilding the bulk-and-cut cycle moved into gym culture and fitness media. In looksmaxxing forums, cutting appears alongside leanmaxxing, the idea that a lean face is a visible part of attractiveness, and threads often ask what a given drop in body fat would do to the face.[5]

The 2014 review by Helms, Aragon and Fitschen for natural bodybuilding contest preparation recommends a rate of loss of roughly 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight per week, protein of about 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean body mass daily, fat at 15 to 30 percent of calories and carbohydrate for the remainder.[9] It judges meal frequency and nutrient timing to have little effect on fat loss or lean-mass retention, lists creatine, caffeine and beta-alanine as beneficial in this context, and suggests that raising carbohydrate modestly near the end of a diet may offset some of the deficit, while noting this has not been formally studied.[9]

A Grokipedia summary lists a daily deficit of about 300 to 500 kcal (roughly 10 to 20 percent below maintenance), avoiding deficits larger than 25 percent, maintained resistance training with progressive loading, two to four cardio sessions a week, and monitoring through photos, tape measurements, strength logs and body-composition scans.[2] It describes mini-cuts as short, more aggressive deficits where much of the early loss is water and glycogen, and refeeds or diet breaks as periodic higher-carbohydrate days or maintenance weeks used to ease hunger and plateaus.[2]

For the final days before a contest, the 2014 review says dehydration and electrolyte manipulation can be dangerous and may not improve appearance, and that carbohydrate loading has a theoretical rationale but is under-studied.[9]

When intake is below expenditure the body draws on stored fat, a process promoted by low insulin and by catecholamines, cortisol and growth hormone.[2] Leptin falls as fat stores shrink, which can raise hunger, and the body can reduce energy expenditure in response to prolonged restriction, a pattern reviewed as metabolic adaptation in a 2014 paper by Trexler, Smith-Ryan and Norton.[2][11] That paper describes changes in hormones, mitochondrial efficiency and expenditure that limit weight loss and offers recommendations for weight reduction and maintenance in athletes.[11]

Resistance training during a deficit is the main way practitioners try to retain muscle. A systematic review of 14 randomised trials compared energy restriction alone with energy restriction plus exercise in adults with obesity and reported that adding exercise increased fat-mass loss and, depending on exercise type, preserved lean body mass and improved strength and fitness.[12]

In a 2011 randomised trial, Garthe and colleagues assigned 24 elite athletes to slow (about 0.7 percent of body weight per week) or fast (about 1.4 percent) weight loss, both with four resistance sessions a week.[11] Body weight fell about 5.5 percent in both groups; fat mass fell 31 percent in the slow group and 21 percent in the fast group, and lean mass rose about 2 percent in the slow group but was unchanged in the fast group.[11] A 12-month follow-up of 23 of these athletes found that fat-mass and lean-mass advantages for the slow group were no longer significantly different between groups by then.[11]

A 2014 review of metabolic adaptation in athletes summarises how energy restriction changes hormones and energy expenditure, and a 2019 narrative review of protein for athletes suggests that higher intakes may help preserve lean mass during energy restriction.[11]

Studies of facial adiposity in observers show the appearance connection: de Jager, Coetzee and Coetzee (2018) reviewed the literature and found perceived facial fat tracks BMI or body fat percentage closely, while Re and Perrett (2014) found participants reduced a face's adiposity more to maximise attractiveness than to maximise perceived leadership.[11] No published trial has tested cutting specifically as a way to change facial attractiveness, and no trial has examined deliberate cuts in adolescents for appearance.

The 2014 contest-preparation review notes that competitors face an elevated risk of eating and body-image disorders and recommends access to appropriate mental-health professionals.[9] A 2017 narrative review of eating disorders in men reports that disordered eating affects a substantial minority of men and that muscularity-oriented attitudes and behaviours are linked to its prevalence and consequences.[13]

Wikipedia's entry on relative energy deficiency in sport describes a syndrome of low energy availability with effects on menstruation, bone density and, in men, androgen levels, strength and mood; it cites a figure of under 30 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day as a level physicians watch for in female athletes, and notes that data on male athletes are limited.[10] A Grokipedia summary lists falling testosterone and thyroid hormones, fatigue, low libido, electrolyte problems, and psychological effects including anxiety, depression, eating-disorder symptoms and muscle dysmorphia among reported risks of aggressive or prolonged cuts.[2]

Forum posts by minors raise a further question, whether a deep deficit during puberty can affect growth or bone mass. No study located addresses cutting in adolescents for appearance, and replies in threads range from caution to the view that a sensible deficit does not affect either.[3][4]

On looksmax.org, users ask how low calories can go while cutting at 16, with one teenager saying they want to cut as aggressively as possible without stunting growth.[3] Another 16-year-old describes cutting from 88 kg to 73 kg over several months and worrying about lost bone mass and height potential; a reply says a sensible deficit does not cause either.[4]

Other threads discuss cutting lowering appetite, carbohydrate restriction and mood, and how much cutting from 16 to 17 percent body fat to 11 to 13 percent would change appearance.[5][7][8] Replies in some of these threads recommend exogenous drugs to speed a cut; this wiki does not give dosing or sourcing for such compounds.

timeline.event: Eugen Sandow stages the Great Competition at the Royal Albert Hall, an early public physique contest [1].
Joe and Ben Weider found the IFBB, which later organised Mr. Olympia [1].
The first Mr. Olympia contest is held [1].
The documentary Pumping Iron brings bodybuilding contest preparation to a wide audience [1].
Garthe and colleagues publish a randomised trial of slow versus fast weight loss in elite athletes [11].
The IOC consensus statement introduces RED-S, and reviews of natural contest preparation and metabolic adaptation in athletes appear [9][10][11].
A review of muscularity-oriented disordered eating in men is published [13].
A review and meta-analysis links perceived facial adiposity to BMI and body fat [11].

lore.intro: Cutting is framed in looksmaxxing forums as the way to reveal facial bone structure and muscle definition, and much of the discussion involves teenagers asking about deficits during puberty.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Cutting during puberty can stunt growth or cost height and bone mass
claims.believers: Teenage posters fear that aggressive cuts will close growth plates early or reduce height potential, while some replies say a moderate deficit does not do this.[3][4]
claims.experts: No study located has examined cutting in adolescents for appearance. Reviews of low energy availability describe bone and hormonal effects in athletes when intake is persistently low.[10]

claims.claim: Dropping to low body fat noticeably improves appearance
claims.believers: Posters ask how much cutting from around 16-17 percent to 11-13 percent would change their looks and report improved definition.[5]
claims.experts: A meta-analysis found perceived facial adiposity tracks BMI and body fat closely, and an experiment found people reduced facial adiposity to maximise attractiveness; no trial has measured attractiveness change from a cut.[11]

claims.claim: Lifting and high protein let you lose fat while keeping muscle
claims.believers: Bodybuilding communities cut with heavy training and high protein so that weight lost is mostly fat.[2]
claims.experts: The 2014 natural-bodybuilding review recommends high protein and gradual loss, and a trial found slower loss produced more fat loss and a lean-mass gain in elite athletes.[9][11]

claims.claim: Slower cuts preserve more muscle than fast ones
claims.believers: Many guides advise about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight per week.[2]
claims.experts: Garthe and colleagues found the slower group gained lean mass and lost more fat, while the faster group's lean mass was unchanged; differences were no longer significant at 12 months.[11]

claims.claim: Aggressive deficits cause muscle loss and hormonal effects
claims.believers: Some posters report that cutting lowered their appetite, and one thread title describes cutting carbs as making the poster depressed.[7][8]
claims.experts: Reviews describe low energy availability as linked to lower androgen levels, bone density and strength in men, though data in men are limited.[10]

claims.claim: Cutting speeds up with added drugs
claims.believers: Some forum replies suggest adding an injectable weight-loss drug to a cut.[3]
claims.experts: This is a separate topic with its own medical literature; no study located tests such use in adolescents.
